extracted.intended_audience: Recipients of Federal financial assistance (K-12 and postsecondary institutions), Title IX coordinators, campus administrators, lawyers and compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements for how recipients must respond to reports and formal complaints of sexual harassment under Title IX, including scope, procedural protections, supportive measures, and documentation obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Title IX coverage (program or activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX coverage depends on the recipient's degree of control and the environment where the harassment occurs; harassment must take place under operations of a funding recipient and in a context subject to the school's control. For responding to sexual harassment, a recipient's "education program or activity" includes circumstances over which the recipient exercised substantial control and may include buildings owned or controlled by a student organization officially recognized by a postsecondary institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation tied to 20 U.S.C. 1687 and 34 CFR 106.2(h),(i); harassment occurring outside an education program/activity may be dismissed for Title IX purposes but can be addressed under other conduct codes. See discussion regarding Clery Act geography vs Title IX coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate indifference standard for liability
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient that did not engage in harassment directly is not liable for damages under Title IX unless its deliberate indifference 'subjects' students to harassment; deliberate indifference must at minimum 'cause [students] to undergo' harassment or 'make them liable or vulnerable' to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the threshold for damages liability (citing Davis and related cases). Recipients must be able to show their response was not deliberately indifferent and must document reasons for that conclusion (§106.45(b)(10)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory dismissal for conduct outside education program/activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mandatory dismissal under §106.45(b)(3)(i) applies when alleged conduct occurred outside an education program or activity, but such dismissal is only for Title IX purposes and does not preclude the recipient from addressing the conduct through other codes of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should ensure alternative disciplinary or conduct processes are available and document any actions taken outside Title IX when dismissal is required under Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer supportive measures to every complainant
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.44(a) requires recipients to promptly offer supportive measures to each complainant; the Title IX Coordinator must engage in an interactive process, consider the complainant's wishes regarding available supportive measures, and explain the process for filing a formal complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures are defined in §106.30. Offering supportive measures is required whether or not a formal complaint is filed. Documentation of the offer and the interactive process is implied best practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable treatment of parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must treat complainants and respondents equitably: equitable treatment means, for example, following a §106.45 grievance process before imposing disciplinary sanctions or other actions that are not 'supportive measures' against a respondent, while offering supportive measures to complainants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The introductory sentence of §106.45(b) requires that any additional provisions a recipient adopts as part of its grievance process must apply equally to both parties. Recipients must avoid favoring one side and ensure parallel application of rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality and freedom from conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: All Title IX Coordinators, investigators, decision-makers, and persons facilitating informal resolution processes must be free from conflicts of interest or bias against complainants and respondents generally or against any individual party, and must receive training that includes how to serve impartially (§106.45(b)(1)(iii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes that a Title IX Coordinator interacting with a respondent in emergency removal situations must likewise serve impartially. Recipients should implement screening, training, and recusal policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to investigate and adjudicate formal complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations specify that when a formal complaint is filed by a complainant or signed by the Title IX Coordinator, the recipient's non-deliberately indifferent response must include investigating and adjudicating the sexual harassment allegations (§106.44(b)(1); §106.30 definition of 'formal complaint'; §106.45(b)(3)(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must have processes in place to receive, investigate, and adjudicate formal complaints and to document steps taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to live hearing and cross-examination; exclusion of untested statements
rubrics_metrics.description: For postsecondary institutions, §106.45(b)(6)(i) requires live hearings to adjudicate formal complaints and provides that either party has the right to a live hearing and cross-examination (which can be conducted in separate rooms). The decision-maker must not rely on the statement of a party or witness who does not submit to cross-examination, resulting in exclusion of statements that remain untested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must design hearing procedures that allow cross-examination by advisors while protecting parties (e.g., separate rooms and technology). Policies should ensure that untested statements are not the basis for determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rape-shield protections (relevance of prior sexual history)
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(6) deems questions and evidence about the complainant's sexual predisposition or prior sexual behavior irrelevant, unless offered to (1) prove someone other than the respondent committed the alleged conduct, or (2) prove consent in relation to specific incidents of the complainant's prior sexual behavior with respect to the respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-makers should exclude irrelevant sexual history evidence except for these narrow exceptions. The rule is categorical with limited exceptions; training and pre-hearing relevance determinations recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileged information restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(1)(x) precludes recipients from using information or evidence protected by a legally recognized privilege in the grievance process unless the privilege holder has waived the privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must identify privileged materials and secure waivers before using such evidence; policies should instruct investigators and decision-makers on privilege determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of non-responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations include a presumption that the respondent is not responsible for the alleged conduct prior to a determination regarding responsibility (§106.45(b)(1)(iv)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must structure investigative and adjudicative procedures to reflect and preserve this presumption; see the dedicated 'Presumption of Non-Responsibility' subsection for further purpose and function guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretionary dismissal where evidence cannot be gathered or matter previously adjudicated
rubrics_metrics.description: One basis for discretionary dismissal of a formal complaint (or allegations therein) is where specific circumstances prevent the recipient from gathering evidence sufficient to reach a determination; likewise, allegations precisely the same as previously investigated and adjudicated may justify dismissal under §106.45(b)(3)(ii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should document the factual basis for exercising discretionary dismissal and ensure dismissal decisions comply with §106.45 and are not applied discriminatorily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility in procedural details (timeframes, technology, evidence sharing, standard of proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations grant recipients flexibility in several areas: recipients may choose how to calculate timeframes (calendar days, school days, etc.); live hearings may be virtual (§106.45(b)(6)(i)); recipients are not required to provide evidence via a file-sharing platform (§106.45(b)(5)(vi)); and recipients may choose between the preponderance of the evidence standard or the clear and convincing standard (§106.45(b)(7)(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must ensure any choices are applied equally to both parties and are documented in policy. Flexibility does not relieve recipients of the core procedural protections required by §106.45.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.71 prohibits retaliation against any individual for exercising rights under Title IX, including the right to participate, or to choose not to participate, in a Title IX grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must adopt and enforce anti-retaliation policies, provide training, and investigate allegations of retaliation promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency removal and administrative leave standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Emergency removals of students must meet the emergency removal standards in §106.44(c); non-student employees may be placed on administrative leave (with or without pay) while a §106.45 grievance process is pending without needing to meet the emergency removal standards (§106.44(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must comply with due process and privacy laws (e.g., FERPA) when executing and disclosing emergency removals; decisions should be individualized and documented, and FERPA may limit disclosures to complainants about emergency removals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process notice and hearing expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Due process principles apply in disciplinary contexts: at minimum, students facing suspension or removal should be given some kind of notice and an opportunity for a hearing appropriate to the nature of the case (citing Goss v. Lopez).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should design notice and hearing procedures practically, consistent with the nature of the sanction and applicable constitutional and statutory requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary meaning of relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations do not define 'relevance' and state that the ordinary meaning of the word should be understood and applied in evaluating evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-makers should apply standard relevance analysis (ordinary meaning) and be prepared to justify relevance rulings in writing where disputes arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation obligation re: non-deliberate indifference
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must document their reasons for concluding that their response to sexual harassment was not deliberately indifferent (§106.45(b)(10)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain contemporaneous written records of assessment, investigatory steps, supportive measures offered, and rationale showing how the response addressed the harassment and prevented recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'determination of responsibility' and 'determination regarding responsibility'
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations use 'determination of responsibility' to describe a finding that the respondent is responsible, and 'determination regarding responsibility' to describe any determination regardless of outcome (responsible or not) — language matters in process descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies and notifications should use precise terminology consistent with the regulations to avoid confusion about outcomes and timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on considering statements that are not subject to cross-examination (hearsay consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although not framed as a hearsay rule, §106.45(b)(6)(i) requires that decision-makers not rely on statements of parties or witnesses who do not submit to cross-examination at a live hearing, effectively excluding untested statements from determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should plan for how to handle situations where a party or witness refuses to submit to cross-examination (e.g., expected exclusion of their statements) and explain these consequences in notices to parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients' locally selected rules must not be sex-discriminatory in application
rubrics_metrics.description: While recipients may adopt their own rules and practices in the grievance process, the manner in which a recipient adopted or applied such a rule could constitute sex discrimination; the entire grievance process must be conducted impartially and free from conflicts of interest or bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing local rules, conduct equity reviews and apply rules equally to both parties; keep records demonstrating equal application to reduce risk of claims of sex discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on finding materially false statements based solely on determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.71(b)(2) cautions that a determination regarding responsibility alone is not sufficient to conclude that a party has made a materially false statement in bad faith; recipients retain discretion to address false statements under their own codes of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should not automatically treat an adverse determination as proof of bad-faith lying and must apply their own code of conduct standards and procedures before imposing sanctions for false statements.
